papers.title: Huge If True: Learning from the Size of the Surprise
papers.abstract: Responses to earnings surprises depend on an unknown multiplier mapping earnings to value. Investors, however, learn about the news and the multiplier from the same number. Large surprises may indicate small multipliers and tiny surprises large ones. We model how greater uncertainty about the multiplier attenuates responses on average but makes them steeper near zero surprises. In an incentivized experiment, we find that greater processing constraints lower average sensitivity but raise it near zero. We confirm this with real-world earnings announcements: stocks with higher valuation uncertainty, our proxy for multiplier uncertainty, respond less on average but more steeply near zero.

papers.title: Human Capital in Context: What Employment Survival Reveals About Worker-Firm Match
papers.abstract: There is no best worker in general, only a best worker for a particular firm. We develop a measure of worker-firm match quality that treats fit as a property of the pair, learned from the survival of employment relationships. A two-tower neural network embeds workers, from their career histories and current positions, and firms, from their characteristics and business descriptions, into a common space, and match quality is the cosine similarity of the two vectors. The measure takes its functional form from the skill-weights model of firm-specific human capital, and its only estimated objective, a separation hazard, from the view of the job match as an experience good. Estimated on more than a billion person-periods covering 101 million workers and 8.4 million firms, a 0.1 increase in match quality lowers the odds of separation by 48%. About a quarter of the variance of match quality is specific to the worker-firm pair, which worker-, firm-, and occupation-level measures set to zero by construction. Workers earn more when better matched, especially early in a relationship, and firms whose workforces score higher grow faster, become more profitable, and are issued more, and more valuable, patents over the next five years than their industry peers. Because it scores pairs that never formed, the measure also predicts where movers go, and acquirers record a larger share of the price as goodwill when the target's workers would fit the acquirer better than they fit the target.

papers.title: Convergence rates for truncated and discretised signature expansions
papers.abstract: Linear expansions in Brownian Stratonovich signatures, which originate in stochastic Taylor expansions, are increasingly used to represent and model processes with memory. Their numerical use requires truncating the signature at a level $M$ and discretising the driving path along $N$ steps. Under a simple growth condition on the coefficients of the linear expansion, we establish strong and weak convergence rates for both approximations, uniformly in time. The strong truncation error decays like $(B^M/(M!)^\varepsilon)^a$ for some constant $B$, uniformly in $N$, where $\varepsilon$ measures the growth of the coefficients and $a$ the regularity of the test function; the weak error does not improve on it. The discretisation error is of order $N^{-a/2}$ in $L^p$, and $N^{-1}$ weakly for polynomial test functions, uniformly in $M$. All these rates are sharp for polynomial test functions, and $M$, $N$ can be chosen independently. We extend the estimates to errors in probability, on distribution functions and on risk measures, and illustrate them on stochastic delay equations, Volterra processes and option pricing in signature volatility models.

papers.title: Data-center growth impacts household electricity costs more through wholesale prices than through grid reinforcement
papers.abstract: Rapid data-center expansion is raising concerns about electricity affordability, yet how the costs of serving these large new loads reach residential customers remains poorly understood. Here, we quantify the potential impact of 371 announced Texas data-center projects, totaling 38.9 GW by 2030, on residential electricity costs by linking power system expansion, wholesale electricity markets, transmission reinforcement, and retail cost allocation. We find that accommodating this demand increases modeled residential electricity costs in one representative case by 1.64 cents/kWh, with 68% arising from higher wholesale electricity prices and 32% from regulated transmission charges. Allowing new gas generation near data centers reduces the 2023 residential cost increase to 0.92 cents/kWh, whereas excluding data centers from the transmission cost-sharing base raises it to 1.87 cents/kWh. These findings reveal that the residential cost burden of data-center growth is driven primarily by wholesale electricity price increases, rather than direct transmission investment costs, and depends critically on generation siting, infrastructure planning, and cost allocation.

papers.title: Novel Esscher concepts for informational risks and valuation in market models under random horizon
papers.abstract: This paper considers the setting constituted by the triplet $(S,\mathbb{F},τ)$. The pair $(S,\mathbb{F})$ is the initial model where $S$ is the discounted price process of risky assets (Stocks) and $\mathbb{F}$ is the ``public" flow of information that is available to all agents over time. $τ$ is an arbitrary random time, which might not be seen through the flow $\mathbb{F}$, and it represents a default time in credit risk and a death time of an insured in life insurance where mortality and/or longevity risks present serious challenges. For simplicity, we suppose $S$ follows a geometric jump-diffusion model with stochastic volatiles and $\mathbb{F}$ is generated by a Brownian motion and Poisson process. In this setting, we address how the Esscher densities and/or measures notions can evolves with the informational risk induced by $τ$. In fact, we introduce the notion of Esscher with degrees-of-freedom associated to the informational risks generated by $τ$. On the one hand, we give various and complete characterizations of these Esscher notions in our informational setting. On the other hand, we fully characterize the Escher-prices bounds, for vulnerable claims (claims built on the occurrence of $τ$), using constrained backward stochastic differential equations (CBSDEs for short hereafter) that appear to be novel as well.

papers.title: On the continuity of martingale optimal transport in higher dimensions
papers.abstract: We investigate qualitative and quantitative continuity of martingale optimal transport under perturbations of both marginals in dimensions $d\geq2$. We assume that each pair of marginals admits a reference martingale coupling whose density relative to the product of its marginals is bounded above and away from zero, uniformly along the sequence. If the limiting target measure is not carried by a hyperplane, we prove continuity under $W_1$-convergence for continuous costs of at most linear growth, assuming only finite first moments. For Lipschitz costs, a uniform $p$-moment bound on the targets, $p>1$, yields an explicit stability estimate with exponent $(1-1/p)/2$; uniformly bounded target supports give exponent $1/2$. The proof constructs a correction of couplings with small martingale bias while preserving both marginals. Truncated moment corrections allow the target measure to have unbounded support. The construction also shows that every martingale coupling of the limiting marginals can be approximated in $W_1$ by martingale couplings of the approximating marginals. We also discuss counterexamples showing that neither the uniform density condition nor non-degeneracy of the limiting target measure can be omitted in general.

papers.title: Accuracy Is Not Welfare: Evaluating AI Buyers under Strategic Price Complexity in a Synthetic Duopoly
papers.abstract: AI buying agents may alter sellers' incentives as well as consumers' decisions. In a synthetic duopoly, we evaluate price-comparison pipelines on a fixed menu and in empirical correlated-equilibrium games. Calculator assistance selects an optimal offer 84.00% of the time, versus 68.57% under verified-total disclosure, yet disclosure has a 20.14-unit higher consumer-worst equilibrium surplus. A frozen-strategy holdout comparison favors disclosure, while re-solving equilibria under scenario resampling produces a range spanning zero. These model-based results show why accuracy, loss severity, seller incentives, and welfare incidence require separate measurement.

papers.title: Verifiable Settlement and Pricing for Local Energy Markets: Architecture and Deployment on Hyperledger Besu
papers.abstract: We implement privacy-preserving local electricity exchanges using an automated market maker on the Hyperledger Besu network under QBFT consensus. The proposed protocol operator collects individual electricity positions off-chain and publishes aggregate supply and demand on the blockchain, where smart contracts compute market prices every fifteen minutes. Individual positions remain off-chain; Poseidon2 commitments and UltraHonk zeroknowledge proofs, generated from Noir circuits, verify aggregation, payments, and daily balance updates. The architecture retains community coordination while making financial execution independently auditable. Signed receipts and member-triggered recourse prevent unverified or partial settlement. In a ten-household experiment using simulated US residential profiles, daily settlement uses approximately 19 million gas and produces eight-member proofs in 2.4 seconds. Over four simulated days, local trading covers 34.4% of demand and reduces grid-only costs by 30.5% under assumed tariffs. Numerically computed __-Nash Equilibrium electricity profiles capture 83-88% of the social planner surplus.

papers.title: Dynamic Scenario-Based Portfolio Optimization for Multi-Asset ETFs
papers.abstract: Portfolio outcomes may depend as much on trading restrictions as on how returns are modeled. We compared historical moving-window returns with conditional scenarios from ARMA--GARCH models and a Student-$t$ copula for 30 U.S.-listed exchange-traded funds. Matched mean--variance and conditional value-at-risk portfolios were evaluated under long-only and limited long--short bounds over 946 sessions. Historical portfolios had higher observed reward--risk ratios in most comparisons, but no paired difference remained significant after multiple-testing adjustment. Conditional scenarios did not consistently reduce realized downside risk. We distinguished changes in target weights from trades required to rebalance holdings after market movements. Relaxing the target-adjustment limit changed exposures, turnover, and some returns more than varying scenario count or seed in the examined tests. These findings suggest that assessments of conditional return inputs should consider portfolio constraints and trading requirements.

papers.title: Price co-movement and price information diverge across Nordic electricity zones after the energy crisis
papers.abstract: After the 2021-2022 energy crisis, day-ahead prices in Nordic bidding zones no longer move together. We ask whether this divergence also changes the information carried by prices. The answer matters for integrating variable renewable energy (VRE), because it can help identify where wind and solar forecasts are worth producing, publishing, and using. We measured the co-movement of each Norwegian and Swedish zone with Germany-Luxembourg (DE-LU) in 2018-2025. We then used a single model, selected on 2024 data, to forecast 2025 prices at 11:00 on the previous day and tested which inputs improved accuracy in each zone. The zones moved alike until 2019, but co-movement diverged in Sweden in 2020 and in Norway in 2021, and the split has persisted. In 2024, four southern zones co-moved strongly with DE-LU (intraday correlations of 0.54-0.71), while four northern zones co-moved weakly (0.25-0.30). Yet price information did not follow this split. Previous-day neighbouring prices reduced mean absolute error by at most 2.2% in any zone, equally in coupled and isolated zones. Removing the transmission system operators' wind and solar forecasts increased mean absolute error by at most 6% in Norway, 8-16% in Sweden, and 31% in DE-LU, and the ordering held in 2024. Within Norway, the value of these forecasts showed no detectable dependence on reservoir filling. The divergence in co-movement was therefore not matched by a divergence in price information, which differed mainly between national generation systems. Thus, a zone's coupling to the continent does not indicate the value of VRE forecasts there.

papers.title: Unequal Rewards and the Direction of Scientific Work: Evidence from U.S. Public Universities
papers.abstract: Research on pay dispersion has long asked whether unequal rewards increase or depress performance. Tournament theory expects stronger effort, while social comparison accounts expect withdrawal. Both perspectives, however, treat performance as a single scale on which workers can be ranked. Scientific work often resists such ordering. Some contributions extend recognized lines of inquiry and can be evaluated against prevailing standards; others revise the frames through which value is judged and become legible only later. We argue that intellectual tournaments more readily reward the first kind of contribution than the second. Pay dispersion may therefore be associated not only with how much scholars produce but also with what kinds of intellectual exploration are encouraged. We test this argument with administrative payroll records for 105,050 tenure-line faculty in 4,839 departments at 93 U.S. public universities from 2004 to 2026, linked to publication histories in OpenAlex. For each department, we estimate a separate pay equation using rank, contract basis, and seniority, then measure the Gini of the salary variation this local ladder cannot explain. Scholars in departments with greater unexplained pay dispersion publish more papers and receive more citations, but their work is less disruptive, less novel, and more conventional. Additional analyses show that compensation premiums above the ladder go disproportionately to scholars with broad collaborations and topical breadth. Although the design cannot fully separate treatment from selection, the evidence shows that inequality is not only a distributional outcome but also an evaluative structure, shaping which forms of knowledge are recognized, rewarded, and reproduced within organizations and communities.

papers.title: Media Trading with Censored Auction Prices: A Stochastic Control and Reinforcement Learning Approach
papers.abstract: In real-time bidding, marketing agencies must balance campaign performance, transaction margins and the use of a finite advertising budget. A key difficulty is that market-clearing prices are typically observed only when bids are successful, so the information available for subsequent decisions depends on the bidding policy. We formulate this problem using a continuous-time stochastic control model with a latent price process. To construct a price signal, we consider parallel exploratory subcampaigns in which bids are randomized subject to an upper bound. Under a stylized cross-sectional sampling model, the resulting price estimator is consistent and satisfies a mean-square error bound of order $N^{-1}$, where $N$ is the number of exploratory observations. We then describe a model-based approach combining forward-equation calibration with Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman policy iteration and a physics-informed neural network, alongside an entropy-regularized actor-critic approach based on observable information in a model-free setting. Synthetic experiments illustrate the estimator and the computational procedures. The framework clarifies the decision and information trade-offs faced by the agency, while distinguishing full-information benchmarks and estimated-price policies from the genuinely partially observed control problem.

papers.title: Improving Algorithmic Trading for BESS on Intraday Electricity Markets through Distributional Price Forecasts
papers.abstract: Grid-scale battery energy storage systems (BESS) are becoming increasingly important in short-term energy markets, where they help balance fluctuations in variable renewable generation. In many countries, the continuous intraday market is the most important wholesale market for BESS to monetize their flexibility. In this paper, we propose an extension to the myopic rolling intrinsic policy that incorporates intraday price forecasts tailored specifically to the BESS trading problem. While a large literature addresses intraday price forecasting, most existing work focuses on volume-weighted prices during the last hours of trading and consequently fails to capture the features most relevant to BESS trading. Our approach addresses this gap by introducing a novel target variable derived from the limit order book and its dynamics. The resulting forecasts are designed to inform the optimization about future profit opportunities while preserving computational efficiency and avoiding the burden of full stochastic optimization. In a realistic high-frequency simulation setting covering 2023 and 2024, our method improves profits by up to 42% over the naive rolling intrinsic formulation. We further analyze the relationship between forecast accuracy, stability, and financial performance, establishing a clear inverse relationship between accuracy and stability. Finally, we find evidence that BESS size and duration jointly influence both overall profitability and the marginal benefit of incorporating forecasts.

papers.title: Price-impact Martingale optimal transport
papers.abstract: Martingale optimal transport (MOT) provides model-independent bounds for option prices calibrated to vanilla options, assuming frictionless trading in the underlying. In this work, we consider the case where dynamic trading incurs quadratic temporary price impact. First, we prove a duality result for the superhedging price. In particular, the primal of the duality relaxes the strict martingale constraint by penalizing the deviation from a specific martingale. Second, for one asset and one trading period, we interpret this price-impact martingale optimal transport (PIMOT) as a weak optimal transport (WOT) problem, and provide a characterization in the spirit of Wasserstein projection. Finally, we justify that PIMOT is an interpolation between MOT and classical optimal transport (OT), and derive the convergence rate to both sides. Numerical examples with SPX option data show how the price bounds per claim depend on the order size.

papers.title: Uncertainty, Volatility, and Renewable Energy Stock Returns: Evidence From Regime‐Dependent and Machine‐Learning Forecasting Models
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines the predictability of renewable energy stock returns under economic, financial, and policy uncertainty within a real‐time forecasting framework. Using monthly data from May 2007 to May 2025, we compare conventional econometric models, shrinkage estimators, machine‐learning algorithms, and regime‐dependent forecasting models using a recursive expanding‐window design. Forecast performance is evaluated using statistical accuracy measures, robustness analyses, and an economic portfolio evaluation. The results show that nonlinear forecasting methods consistently outperform conventional linear benchmarks. Gradient boosting achieves the lowest forecast errors, while principal component regression provides stable performance across alternative evaluation designs. Regime‐dependent forecasting models improve directional prediction during periods of heightened financial uncertainty but generate more modest gains in forecast accuracy. Predictor‐importance analysis identifies financial‐market volatility as the dominant source of forecasting information, followed by oil‐market volatility and broader policy uncertainty. Overall, the findings demonstrate that combining multiple sources of uncertainty with flexible forecasting methods improves both statistical forecasting performance and the economic value of investment decisions. papers.title: Local Returns and Beliefs about the Stock Market
papers.abstract: Abstract We show that investors extrapolate from recent stock returns of locally headquartered firms when forming beliefs about aggregate stock market outcomes. While it may be optimal to rely on local information, these effects are unrelated to how informative local returns are on predictions of aggregate outcomes. Evidence from a sample of retail investors suggests this belief extrapolation is driven by investors’ own holdings of local firms. Our findings suggest that beliefs about information contained in public signals vary systematically with geography, and are an important component of local biases in equity markets.

papers.title: Realized annual price dispersion, trading activity, and contemporaneous price returns on the Amman Stock Exchange
papers.abstract: Type of the article: Research ArticleAbstractThis study examines how realized annual price dispersion and trading activity co-moved with 2025 price returns in the cross-section of Amman Stock Exchange (ASE) equities. The official yearly sector bulletin contains 160 valid securities; transparent activity and data-validity filters yield a 142-stock baseline sample. Cross-sectional OLS models use HC3 standard errors and are complemented by broad-sector controls, outlier-resistant estimation, alternative range scaling, sample sensitivity, signed range decomposition, and a manual corporate-action audit of extreme observations. The annual high-low range is strongly positively associated with same-year price return: its baseline coefficient is 0.883 (HC3 SE = 0.075). Scaling the range by average price leaves the coefficient positive but reduces R2 from .729 to .307. Decomposing the previous-close-scaled range produces an upside coefficient of 0.806 (SE = 0.071) and a downside coefficient of –0.630 (0.187), with equality strongly rejected (Wald χ2 = 72.61, p &lt; .001). The extreme-observation audit identifies official 2025 capital reductions for PHNX, OFTC, NAQL, and DAFI. Excluding these four securities leaves the unsigned range coefficient positive at 0.850 (0.082; N = 138); the signed coefficients remain 0.792 (0.062) and –0.653 (0.186), respectively. Because return and range are constructed from the same annual price path, these results document robust contemporaneous directional co-movement rather than an ex-ante risk premium, causal liquidity effect, or forecasting relation.AcknowledgmentsThe author thanks the Amman Stock Exchange for making public yearly trading bulletins available. papers.title: Conformal Prediction Intervals for Daily Equity Returns Under Volatility Regimes
papers.abstract: Risk reports rely on interval forecasts, yet parametric volatility models lose their nominal coverage when markets turn turbulent. We ask whether distribution-free conformal prediction can give dependable one-step-ahead intervals for daily equity returns across volatility regimes. Under one online protocol we compare an unconditional Gaussian benchmark, Gaussian and Student-t GARCH(1,1) intervals, a volatility-scaled split conformal predictor, and adaptive conformal inference, alongside five machine learning interval methods, on four European indices and the S&P 500 from 1990 to 2026. The unconditional benchmark overcovers yet covers only about 85 percent of high-volatility days. The GARCH intervals are efficient and well calibrated; the conformal methods give the most accurate marginal coverage and the best coverage on turbulent days. Significance tests and a sensitivity analysis confirm that volatility-scaled conformal correction is most reliable in turbulence, at a small cost in width. Laporan risiko bergantung pada prakiraan interval, tetapi model volatilitas parametrik kehilangan cakupan nominalnya ketika pasar bergejolak. Kami menguji apakah prediksi konformal yang bebas distribusi dapat memberikan interval satu langkah ke depan yang andal untuk imbal hasil saham harian di berbagai rezim volatilitas. Di bawah satu protokol daring, kami membandingkan tolok ukur Gaussian tak bersyarat, interval GARCH(1,1) Gaussian dan Student-t, prediktor konformal terbelah berskala volatilitas, dan inferensi konformal adaptif, bersama lima metode interval berbasis pembelajaran mesin, pada empat indeks Eropa dan indeks S&P 500 dari 1990 hingga 2026. Tolok ukur tak bersyarat memiliki cakupan berlebih secara keseluruhan, namun hanya mencakup sekitar 85 persen hari bervolatilitas tinggi. Interval GARCH efisien dan terkalibrasi baik, sedangkan metode konformal memberikan kalibrasi marginal paling akurat dan cakupan terbaik pada hari bergejolak. Uji signifikansi dan analisis sensitivitas menegaskan bahwa koreksi konformal berskala volatilitas paling andal saat bergejolak, dengan biaya lebar yang kecil.

papers.title: Dispersion in Analysts’ Target Prices and Stock Returns in the Korean Stock Market
papers.abstract: This study examines the relationship between the dispersion in analysts' target prices and stock returns for firms listed on the KOSPI and KOSDAQ markets. We find that analyst target price dispersion is positively and significantly associated with next-month stock returns in panel regressions and Fama-MacBeth cross-sectional regressions, and this relation remains robust after controlling for a variety of firm characteristics. To explore the mechanism underlying this association, we divide the sample into subsamples based on firm size, volatility, turnover, and analyst coverage, and conduct the same analyses within each subsample. The results indicate that the positive relation between target price dispersion and returns is stronger for firms that are smaller, have lower volatility or lower turnover, and receive higher analyst coverage. Overall, our findings suggest that dispersion in analysts' target prices reflects uncertainty about firms' future value and contains additional information beyond traditional risk measures in environments with information frictions.

Secondary data cover 29 companies during 2022–2024, yielding 87 observations. Multiple regression and moderated regression analysis were conducted using SPSS. Both calendar-related return measures show positive associations with stock returns: January B = 0.113 (p < 0.001) and Monday B = 0.093 (p = 0.014). papers.title: Beyond Risk-Adjusted Returns: Tail Risk and Portfolio Implications in Global REITs
papers.abstract: This study compares the performance of major global REIT markets with REITs classified by their geographic operating market and returns measured in the corresponding local currency. The analysis evaluates risk-adjusted performance, dependence structures, downside risk, and portfolio implications using Sharpe, Sortino, Omega, VaR, CVaR, and three portfolio optimization techniques. Results show substantial variation in return distributions and downside risk across markets, while correlations generally increase during the COVID-19 pandemic and the subsequent period. Canadian and Euro-area REITs exhibit comparatively strong risk-adjusted performance, although their tail-risk profiles differ. Portfolio results further show that concentration, volatility, and tail risk do not necessarily produce identical rankings: the most concentrated tangency portfolio generates the highest Sharpe ratio while also exhibiting the most favorable historical VaR and CVaR among the optimized portfolios. The findings demonstrate that global REIT markets remain heterogeneous despite increasing integration and that portfolio evaluation benefits from jointly considering conventional performance, diversification, and tail risk.

papers.title: Cryptocurrency Portfolio Optimization Under Volatility and Tail Risk
papers.abstract: Cryptocurrency markets combine persistent volatility, heavy tails, and recurrent stress episodes. This study asks whether portfolio optimization is sufficient to manage these risks for Bitcoin, Ethereum, Binance Coin, Solana, and XRP, using 1454 daily observations from January 2022 to January 2026. Student-t GARCH and DCC-GARCH forecasts feed static and rolling allocation rules, evaluated out of sample and net of transaction costs against equal-weight, minimum-variance, risk-parity, and minimum-CVaR benchmarks; downside risk is backtested with Kupiec and Christoffersen tests, and three anomaly detectors are validated against four crisis windows, including expanding-window refits. Volatility persistence ranges from 0.912 to 1.000, and average conditional correlations are higher inside four crisis windows than outside (0.76 vs. 0.66), a contrast that exceeds placebo windows but is small relative to neighbouring days. In sample, maximum-Sharpe weights raise the Sharpe ratio (0.88 vs. 0.76) without statistical significance; out of sample, their point estimate is lower than that of equal weighting (0.92 vs. 1.15), a difference that is statistically inconclusive. Risk-based rules cut volatility by about 19% and maximum drawdown by 10 points, whereas GARCH–DCC allocation adds turnover without further gains, and minimum-CVaR cannot be distinguished from minimum-variance allocation in this sample, the tests having limited power. Isolation Forest flags are about 8 times more concentrated in crisis windows than chance, and about 10 times when refitted on an expanding window. Optimization lowers risk, whereas evidence that it improves risk-adjusted performance is inconclusive.

papers.title: The Impact of the US Equity Market Movements on Overnight Returns in the Indian Stock Market: The Moderating Role of Market Volatility.
papers.abstract: This paper studies the relationship between returns in the US equity market and opening gaps in the subsequent Indian Nifty 50. The relationship is studied while also considering whether the relationship varies during periods of high expected US equity volatility. Daily closing and opening prices for the S&P 500 and Nifty 50 are used in conjunction with closing values for the Cboe Volatility Index (VIX). A sample of 239 eligible days is created from 2025 data. The relationship is then examined using correlation, simple linear regression, directional agreement, and average opening gap. For the overall sample, there is a positive correlation (0.386) and R² of 0.149. This means that the fitted linear relationship explains roughly 14.9% of the variation in the opening gaps for the Indian Nifty 50. For days with high VIX values, there is a higher correlation (0.433) and R² of 0.188 compared to the other days, which have values of 0.288 and 0.083, respectively. The level of directional agreement, however, is similar at 63.9% and 63.5% for the high and the other days, respectively. This analysis suggests a positive relationship between the returns in the US equity market and the subsequent opening gaps in Indian equities. The relationship appears to be stronger during high volatility days. A sensitivity check shows that part of the strength of the fitted relationship comes from one unusually large observation: the Indian trading day of 7 April 2025, matched to the US session of 4 April 2025. However, these results are merely descriptive and do not imply causality, statistical significance, or the ability to forecast out of sample.

papers.title: An Empirical Pricing of Interest and Exchange Rate Risk-Premia Over A Cross-Section of Portfolio Returns in Nigeria
papers.venue: International Journal of Social Science and Human Research
papers.abstract: This study examines whether interest rate and exchange rate exposures command risk premia across Nigerian equity portfolios. Six value-weighted portfolios are formed through independent size and book-to-market sorts using monthly price returns from July 2016 to December 2025. A two-pass framework combines time-series exposure regressions with Fama-MacBeth cross-sectional pricing tests. Newey-West statistics and a separately reported Shanken correction assess inference, while equity factors provide benchmark comparisons. Interest rate exposure is significantly negative for several portfolios in the macro-only specification; significant exchange rate exposure is confined to one portfolio. These relationships generally weaken after equity-factor controls. Neither macroeconomic risk commands a statistically significant cross-sectional premium after correcting for estimated-beta uncertainty. Estimated premia change sign when the cross-sectional intercept is restricted, and rolling estimates indicate changing exposures. The findings distinguish portfolio sensitivity from reliable compensation for bearing risk. Investors should monitor interest rate and currency exposures alongside conventional equity risks without assuming that additional exposure generates higher expected returns. The small portfolio cross section, exclusion of dividends and measurement limitations qualify the conclusions.

papers.title: Long Memory in Brazilian Stock Returns and Volatility: Evidence from Book-to-Market Portfolios Across the COVID-19 Period
papers.venue: International Journal of Economics and Finance
papers.abstract: Whether book-to-market characteristics influence long-memory dynamics remains an open question, particularly in emerging equity markets and during periods of systemic stress. This study investigates long-memory dynamics in Brazilian stock returns and volatility and examines whether persistence differs across book-to-market (BTM) portfolios before, during, and after the COVID-19 pandemic. Using daily data (roughly 2,500 observations per stock) for ten highly liquid IBOVESPA stocks from January 2016 to December 2025, we estimate the fractional integration parameter (d) using the semiparametric Geweke-Porter-Hudak (GPH) estimator for the full sample, three subperiods, and rolling windows. The sample comprises ten selected stocks and does not represent the entire Brazilian equity market. The subperiod and rolling-window estimates describe variation in persistence across regimes and over time. The results show little evidence of long memory in returns, which remain broadly consistent with weak-form market efficiency despite a temporary increase in persistence during the pandemic. In contrast, volatility exhibits strong and pervasive long-memory behavior, with persistence intensifying substantially during the COVID-19 crisis before declining only gradually afterward. No systematic differences are found between Low- and High-BTM portfolios in either returns or volatility, suggesting that persistence is driven primarily by firm-specific sources of uncertainty rather than by book-to-market classification. Overall, the evidence indicates that long memory in the Brazilian equity market is more evident in volatility than in returns.

papers.title: A Review of Methods for Predicting Stock Volatility: A Comparison of Traditional Econometric Models, Implied Volatility, and Machine Learning Methods
papers.abstract: Stock volatility forecasting serves as a crucial underpinning for derivatives pricing, asset allocation, and risk management. This paper examines volatility proxy variables, empirical applications, as well as forecasting evaluation metrics, and then reviews representative models and empirical evidence across three research pathways. The comparison concerns the information basis and forecasting horizon, taking into account explanatory power, stability, and economic value. A comprehensive review of the literature suggests that traditional models remain a robust benchmark in scenarios with limited data, in which emphasis is placed on interpretability and reproducibility. Implied volatility can provide incremental information beyond historical data; however, its predictive power is influenced by variance risk premiums, liquidity, and maturity matching. Machine learning offers greater flexibility in high-dimensional data environments, but its advantages depend on rigorous time-series validation and control of information leakage. Because of inconsistencies in proxy variables, loss functions, sample partitioning, and market conditions, existing evidence fails to support the universal superiority of any single method across all tasks. Future analysis should conduct cross-market tests under a unified evaluation framework and integrate statistical forecasting accuracy with economic value in risk management and investment decision-making.

papers.title: Volatility of Selected Macroeconomic Factors on Stock Market Returns in Kenya
papers.abstract: Economic indicators such as money supply, gross domestic product growth, inflation, and interest rates for firms in the Nairobi Stock Exchange 25 index series have fluctuated over the last decade, posing a risk of severe capital flight by foreign investors. This study examined stock return variation and selected macroeconomic variables. A longitudinal panel data design was deployed to assess the mean effects of the selected economic indicators on stock returns. The study further estimated conditional variance and volatility persistence of stock market returns using a Generalized Autoregressive Conditional Heteroskedasticity model. The study selected firms from the Nairobi Stock Exchange 25 index series, which tracks the performance of 25 listed companies based on criteria such as market capitalization, liquidity, and trading activity. Positivist research philosophy guided the analysis. The study drew on capital asset pricing theory and Fisher’s effect theory. The study used census techniques because it included all firms in the index series. The study covered the period 2015 to 2025. The researcher collected secondary data using a data extraction table. The researcher conducted relevant diagnostic tests to assess data reliability. The researcher analyzed observations using descriptive statistics, particularly the mean and standard deviation. To adhere to ethical considerations, the researcher used the gathered data only for the intended objectives. The study showed an overall statistically significant model, with an R-squared of 0.9456 and an Adjusted R-squared of 0.9439, indicating that these variables explain nearly 95% of the variation in stock returns. Consequently, the results revealed a positive, significant correlation between money supply, GDP growth, and stock returns. Similarly, the inflation interest rate was negatively and significantly correlated with stock returns. The GARCH results showed an ARCH effect of 0.505 and a GARCH effect of 0.213, yielding overall persistence of approximately 0.7, with 0.72 as the constant. The results underscore the critical role of macroeconomic stability in shaping stock market outcomes. Economic expansion and liquidity growth boost investor returns, while inflation and high interest rates reduce profitability. This suggests that policymakers should prioritize maintaining low inflation and stable interest rates while fostering economic growth to support a favorable investment climate.

papers.title: Doing Better at Doing Good: Lessons from a Bayesian Meta-Analysis After 20 Years of Poverty Graduation Programs

Third, programs implemented from 2016 onward perform considerably better than those implemented prior to 2016: benefit-cost ratios from 2016 onward are 5.39, compared to 2.89 through 2015. Neither changes in cost nor in high-level design (components) explain this upward trend. Considering other heavily studied interventions, the results show a similar upward trend for treatment effects on behavior change from financial education but not for unconditional cash transfers. papers.title: Beyond Financial Conditions: Measuring Structural Vulnerabilities in the U.S. Financial System
papers.abstract: We introduce the Financial Vulnerability Index (FVI), a novel indicator of financial vulnerabilities in the U.S. Unlike financial condition indices, which measure current credit market conditions and spike during periods of financial turmoil, the FVI displays the gradual build-up of structural financial weaknesses and declines as such episodes materialize. We demonstrate that the FVI exhibits properties consistent with theoretical mechanisms of financial vulnerabilities. When the index is high, adverse shocks are substantially amplified, generating larger declines in consumption and investment. We provide new empirical evidence that monetary tightening is associated with gradual declines in the FVI, with this effect substantially delayed, taking a few years to fully materialize. papers.title: Artificial Intelligence and the U.S. Economy: Current Evidence
papers.abstract: We assess the current evidence on how AI-related investment and the use of AI are affecting the U.S. macroeconomy. Specifically, we document the boom in data center capital investment, the current rate of adoption of AI tools in the economy, the impact of the AI-related investment surge on prices, and discuss whether AI tools have affected the labor market and productivity yet. AI adoption is growing rapidly both among consumers and firms, though most firms are currently not using AI very intensively or at all. AI model-producing firms have also grown extremely fast, and now account for a noticeable fraction of software industry gross output. Prices have climbed in sectors that provide direct inputs to the data centers, such as memory chips. Effects on the labor market so far appear small and somewhat mixed. Similarly, the effects of AI on aggregate productivity growth also appear to be small so far, and the recent pickup in productivity likely reflects factors that predated the diffusion on generative AI.

papers.title: Premiums or Peril
papers.abstract: Using fine-grained data on 465,000 Florida home sales over twelve years and semiparametric machine learning methods, we examine how home prices respond to weather-related risk factors. papers.title: Vigilance, Risk Vulnerability, and the Precautionary Augment
papers.abstract: Risk raises the expected marginal utility of a prudent agent. We define this proportional change as the precautionary augment, which measures risk-induced changes in the marginal value of saving, the Lucas Tree risk-free rate, and asset prices in a derivative-saturated market where market-state securities provide incomplete coverage against idiosyncratic risk. One agent is more vigilant than another if their precautionary augment is larger for all unfair risks. We derive and compare conditions for greater vigilance, showing how to implement the Diffidence Theorem geometrically. Because risk vulnerability is equivalent to decreasing vigilance, classic results about risk vulnerability emerge as corollaries.

papers.title: The Flight to Affordability: Effects of Pandemic Rent Increases on Renters By Geography
papers.abstract: In the pandemic era, people moved from high-density, expensive areas to more affordable areas, putting upward pressure on local housing prices. We examine the geographic distribution of rent growth during this time and its effects on renters. We use administrative new lease data from RealPage and household-level data on rent and income from the American Community Survey. We analyze rents and incomes using Public Use Microdata Areas grouped in two ways: by prepandemic rent levels and by pre-pandemic rent-to-income ratios. Rents grew more in areas with lower pre-pandemic rents but not in areas with lower rent-to-income ratios, consistent with higher-income remote workers moving away from high rent areas to more affordable areas. Lower-income households experienced larger increases in rent relative to their income compared to the median renter. However, area-level rent-to-income ratios reflect both compositional changes in renter populations from mobility and changes in local rents. We highlight the need for future work to track affordability for the same households over time to fully understand pandemic era affordability trends.

papers.title: (In)Credible Development RCTs: False Discoveries, Low Power, and a Solution
papers.abstract: We study the statistical credibility of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) in development economics and the optimal allocation of resources to replication. Using 745 principal-hypothesis tests from 190 articles in leading economics journals, we find that actual t-statistics peak well below the theoretical benchmark of 2.8 expected under 80 percent power, though above values associated with p-hacking. This suggests many RCTs are underpowered. Estimating an empirical Bayes mixture model that accounts for selective publication, we find that approximately 30 percent of published rejections are false discoveries, with average directional power at only 40 percent. At conventional significance thresholds, the posterior probability of a false discovery reaches 66 percent. Doubling original sample sizes lowers the average false discovery rate by five percentage points, whereas tightening the significance threshold to 0.005 yields a larger reduction at the cost of total discoveries. Finally, we characterize a funder’s optimal replication policy under a fixed budget and an evidence standard. Under standard regularity conditions, replications concentrate in an intermediate interval of original test statistics, and the optimal replication sample size is single-peaked in the original t-statistic. Illustrative calibrations show that successful replications reduce aggregate false discovery rates to 1.8–7.8 percent, depending on the evidence standard.

papers.title: Measuring Consumption with Credit Card Data: Benchmarking and Beyond
papers.abstract: We introduce a novel monthly county-level consumption dataset constructed from spending data on over 350 million credit cards in the Federal Reserve’s Y-14M reports, covering over 3,000 U.S. counties since 2014. papers.title: Risks and Uncertainty in Monetary Policy
papers.abstract: Central banks monitor macroeconomic risk through two traditions: scenario analysis, regularly used since the mid-1990s, and distributional forecasting, practiced since the late 1960s. The Scenario Synthesis assigns weights to scenarios consistent with the reference distribution, offering a practical and reproducible tool for risk assessment and policy deliberation under deep uncertainty.

papers.title: TaskNet: Building Occupational Task Inventories from Worker Interviews at Scale
papers.abstract: Understanding how AI is reshaping work requires an accurate account of the tasks workers perform. Workers are often the first to see how their jobs are changing, as new responsibilities and tools often appear in everyday work before these changes reach formal descriptions. Interviews with workers can help capture these emerging changes in job tasks. Yet existing methods support standardized ratings across workers, while open-ended conversations with workers remain costly to collect and synthesize at scale. We introduce the Stanford Task Network (TaskNet), an occupational taxonomy grounded directly in workers’ accounts of their everyday work. To construct TaskNet, we develop a mixed-initiative system that induces task inventories directly from workers. The system conducts interviews, standardizes reports into individual task lists, and aggregates these lists into occupational task inventories. Applied to six occupations spanning a range of education requirements and AI exposure, our system interviews 132 workers and produces 202 task statements from 2726 reports, all of which were accepted by O*NET Center analysts, compared to roughly 65%of workers’ write-in task suggestions collected through the current O*NET data collection process, a major alternative source for emerging tasks. Every statement is validated by 318 incumbents in 7923 ratings of relevance and importance. Relative to the task data from the O*NET 31.0 database for the sampled occupations, TaskNet covers 75% of the 118 published O*NET tasks and adds 79 tasks with no O*NET counterpart and 58 that refine existing statements. It covers 89% of tasks reported by held-out workers, compared with 79% for O*NET, and a larger share of the activities described in employer job postings (72.5% vs. 70.2%). Downstream, TaskNet changes AI exposure estimates in both directions, raising them for Software Developers and Lawyers, two occupations where AI’s effects are widely debated. Because such estimates guide workforce policy and training, more complete and up-to-date task lists can help direct these efforts toward the workers most likely to be affected. TaskNet provides a foundation for keeping occupational information current and grounded in workers’ experiences as AI reshapes work.

papers.title: Linear and Nonlinear Econometric Models versus Machine-Learning Models: Evidence from Realized-Volatility Forecasting(Revised)
papers.abstract: This paper examines which representations of persistence and nonlinearity are most useful for forecasting realized volatility and whether machine learning adds value beyond econometric models designed for long memory and regime dependence. We compare HAR, ARFIMA, threshold HAR, smooth-transition HAR, and Markov-switching HAR with XGBoost and several neural-network models for the S&P 500 and 40 U.S. equities. Models are evaluated under a baseline information set using realized-volatility history and an extended set of predictors selected by Elastic Net. Forecast performance is assessed using MSFE, MAE, QLIKE, Model Confidence Sets, Diebold–Mariano tests, realized utility, and filtered-historical-simulation VaR and expected shortfall. The results reveal a robust horizon-dependent ranking: Markov-switching HAR performs best at short horizons, ARFIMA generally leads at the monthly horizon, and the five-day horizon is intermediate. Machine-learning models sometimes improve on HAR but do not systematically outperform the broader econometric set. These findings are robust across estimation windows, re-estimation frequencies, richer information sets, log-volatility targets, and individual equities; stock-level results are also robust to an alternative realized-volatility measure. Overall, forecast performance depends primarily on capturing the persistence and nonlinear dynamics most relevant at each horizon.

papers.title: The Impact of Climate Change on Fisheries
papers.abstract: This paper provides the first causal estimate of the effect of ocean temperature variations on fishing revenue. We develop a simple theoretical model underpinning an empirical specification estimated on 2.5 million spatially explicit observations of fishing revenue from all European vessels for 2013–2022. The identification strategy leverages a novel metric, Marine Degree Days, which quantifies species-specific temperature exposure relative to biologically established thermal tolerance intervals. Within this framework we address key identification challenges, including spatial selection and ecological interdependencies across species. We find that deviations from species’ thermal preferences lead to significant losses in fishing revenue, with heat exposure causing the most pronounced impacts. These effects are mediated by species’ vertical mobility and ecological characteristics. Projections across different climate scenarios point to widespread revenue declines by 2100, reaching €560 million annual losses in the warmest scenario, though impacts are highly spatially heterogeneous. Lower-income, equatorial areas are expected to suffer the most, while some colder regions experience gains.

papers.title: Policy Evaluation Beyond Significance Testing: Evidence from Chicago's ShotSpotter Contract
papers.abstract: Program impact estimates that are not statistically significant are often treated as providing little guidance for policy choice, even when economically important effects remain plausible. In such cases, the decision-relevant task is not simply to test whether the effect differs from zero, but to estimate the probability distribution of programmatic effects. The importance of going beyond hypothesis testing is especially clear when evaluations are underpowered relative to the effect needed for benefits to exceed costs. We illustrate this point using Chicago’s contract for ShotSpotter, an acoustical gunshot detection system that reduces police response times and may therefore have improved survival among shooting victims. Using a geographic RD design, we estimate that ShotSpotter reduced the shooting fatality rate by 2.5 percentage points, equivalent to roughly 49 fewer deaths per year. Although the estimate is not statistically significant, its implied benefit far exceeds the cost of the service. To have enough statistical power under the hypothesis testing approach to detect an effect of this size would require 87 years’ worth of Chicago shooting data. We instead implement a decision-relevant perspective using Bayesian analysis, treating the life-saving effect as a random variable. We find positive expected net benefits, with posterior probabilities that benefits exceed costs ranging from 70% under a flat prior and a $0.5 million value of statistical life to 99.6% under a no-harm prior and a $13.6 million value. The results illustrate how reliance on statistical significance can discard decision-relevant evidence when economically meaningful effects are difficult to detect precisely.

papers.title: Unconventional Monetary Policy and Deposit Retention
papers.abstract: The two dimensions of unconventional monetary policy — holding the short rate at the zero-lower bound (ZLB) and quantitative easing (QE) — shifted deposit composition toward more interest-sensitive customers. The ZLB drew these customers by creating rate compression, which limited the benefit of searching for high-yielding liquidity sources. QE also drew rate-sensitive, large depositors from the Federal Reserve’s purchases of bonds from non-banks. Once policy normalized, flow sensitivity and the deposit beta both increased with exposure to QE and the ZLB. We conclude that unconventional monetary policy made deposit retention costlier and riskier for banks.

papers.title: Debiasing Law Enforcement Officers: Evidence from an Expressive Arts Intervention in India
papers.abstract: Frontline state agents exercise substantial discretion over citizens’ access to public services, yet little is known about whether the attitudes and beliefs shaping this discretion can be changed among incumbent bureaucrats. Partnering with the Bihar Police - one of India’s largest states that operates under comparatively severe policing capacity constraints, we conduct a cluster randomized controlled trial across 417 police stations and roughly 2,500 active duty senior field police officers to evaluate a three-day expressive arts intervention, grounded in the Theatre of the Oppressed, designed to change police responses to gender-based violence (GBV). Approximately 7 months after baseline, treated officers exhibit more favorable attitudes toward GBV, greater empathy, and stronger legal knowledge. These changes translate into observed policing behavior: in standardized victim audits conducted one year later, officers in treated stations are 15 percentage points less likely to blame victims, dismiss fewer complaints, and provide more referrals, while administrative records show a 41 percent reduction in registration delays and, over a longer horizon, increased GBV reporting by citizens. Exploiting variation generated by officer transfers, we find suggestive evidence that these effects persist when treated officers relocate and diffuse to untreated officers working alongside treated colleagues. The effects also extend to the workplace: junior female officers working with treated senior officers report lower harassment and anxiety. These findings show that the attitudes shaping bureaucratic discretion are malleable and that changing how incumbent state agents exercise authority can improve both citizen-facing service delivery and the broader workplace environment.

The preferred specifications place much of the systematic variation in policy-rate forecasts in intercepts that vary across forecast horizons and survey dates. Evidence of "changing perceptions" of monetary policy via economically meaningful time-varying response coefficients is weak overall.

papers.title: The Hidden Sharpe Ratio
papers.abstract: We estimate the maximal Sharpe ratio in large cross-sections of assets directly, without constructing the efficient portfolio. Covariance estimation in this setting requires regularization, which suppresses the contribution of small-eigenvalue directions. Our estimator progressively recovers this contribution, yielding tight upper and lower bounds with asymptotic confidence intervals. We further show that ridge-regularized Markowitz portfolios, the construction underlying many existing high-Sharpe benchmarks, deliver out-of-sample Sharpe ratios that fall short of the true maximum by an explicit, non-vanishing multiplicative factor. Applied to U.S. equities, the method delivers an estimated maximal annualized Sharpe ratio of approximately 7.4, or 5.0 once micro-cap stocks are excluded, substantially exceeding existing portfolio-based benchmarks of 1.0–4.0. Adding corporate bonds raises the maximum, though not by a statistically significant margin. Nonlinear portfolio weights dominate linear ones, and characteristics introduced after 2004 contribute little additional Sharpe ratio.

papers.title: AI as Shared Business Infrastructure: Firm Growth and the Distribution of Gains
papers.abstract: Generative AI improves performance on individual tasks, but whether those gains translate into firm growth, and for which firms, remains an open question. We study a leading Chinese e-commerce platform that in 2024 embedded a generative AI system in the operating software firms use to run their businesses, drawing on centrally developed models and platform-wide data to deliver ready-to-use applications to every firm. Complete records of each firm’s AI use, linked to its monthly operations and sales, let us trace adoption through changes in business capabilities, such as reaching customers and introducing new products, to sales growth. Using a matched difference-in-differences design and focusing on firms with annual sales below RMB 5 million, we find that adoption raises monthly sales by 51.6%, primarily through a 47.0% increase in the number of orders; instrumental-variable estimates confirm these results. Adopters reach more customers, update their product lines faster, and deliver better product and service quality, with the largest proportional gains for the smallest firms. Two mechanisms help explain the results. First, AI lowers the cost of routine work: adopters produce more product content and change listings more often while spending less staff time per order, and the gains are largest for firms that faced the highest costs relative to sales before adoption. Second, AI reduces information frictions: adopters post richer product information, and the gains are largest in markets where demand is hard to predict and matching quality is poor, especially for small firms. At the market level, product categories with greater pre-existing information frictions see more sales by existing firms, more entry, and more new products. AI expands markets rather than merely shifting sales from non-adopters to adopters.

papers.title: Sorting by Participation: A Field Experiment in a Stem-cell Registry
papers.abstract: Unavailability of stem-cell donors at the confirmatory typing (CT) stage, an operational milestone in the stem-cell donation process, reduces the effective supply of life-saving transplants for blood cancer patients worldwide. Although (potential) donors register voluntarily, requests may come much later, when circumstances and commitment have changed; keeping registered donors engaged and identifying who will follow through are therefore central managerial questions for registries. In a field experiment with a leading stem-cell registry, we randomize the framing of routine invitations to an engagement initiative. Relative to a business-as-usual letter, our experimental letters present the registry’s requests more saliently; two of them add identity framings inviting donors to join a “quickly available” or a “highly committed” donor team. The salience and identity framings significantly reduce initiative participation compared to the business-as-usual rate, yet intention-to-treat analyses show no detectable effect on average CT availability. Our central finding is that participation sorts donors by reliability: participants are unavailable in 12% of cases, versus 30% of non-participants. From a managerial perspective, opting in works as a reliability flag. Prioritizing participants in our experimental arms implies a relative increase of up to 7.5% more one-year survivors compared to not using this flag. Gains from flagging are likely to be larger for registries with lower availability.

papers.title: Inattentive Price Setting and Inflation Under Fiscal Policy Uncertainty
papers.abstract: How do high public debt and fiscal uncertainty interact to shape inflation? Higher debt raises steady-state taxes, affecting attention through two opposing forces. While these taxes reduce the profit stakes of mispricing, they make desired prices more sensitive to tax fluctuations, increasing the value of information. The interaction generates a U-shaped relationship between public debt and attention, and therefore between debt and inflation volatility. Using euro-area firm-level expectations data, we document that the passthrough of expected input-cost growth into expected selling-price growth rises systematically with a country's debt-to-GDP ratio, consistent with the model. In the calibrated general-equilibrium model, an increase in debt from 100% to 175% of GDP raises inflation volatility by about 20%, mainly because firms reallocate attention toward fiscal shocks.

papers.title: Target What? The Foundations of Poverty Targeting
papers.abstract: Most government transfer programs aim to target the poor. Doing so implicitly assumes that the lowest-consumption households have the highest marginal social valuation, i.e., have the highest social welfare gain from an additional dollar. But this need not be the case. In 600 Indonesian villages, we ask over 5,500 villagers to rank other villagers on how well off they are and how much a modest cash transfer would help them, and compare these rankings to consumption and self-assessed welfare. Targeting consumption misses 77% of households with the highest marginal social valuation. Targeting self-assessed welfare misses 57%. Even targeting those the community ranks worst off in levels, not margins, misses 25%. Divergences between different notions of neediness are statistically predictable. In a randomized controlled trial, proxy means tests best target consumption, self-targeting ordeals capture self-assessed welfare levels, and community targeting comes closest to marginal social valuation. Targeting strategies inescapably embed normative stances.

papers.title: The Main Monetary Policy Shock
papers.abstract: We propose a novel procedure to identify a main monetary policy (MMP) shock as the linear combination of monetary policy surprises that best explains macroeconomic fluctuations. Implemented with two standard high-frequency yield-curve surprises and the Boehm and Kroner (2024) non-yield shock, the MMP shock explains nontrivial business-cycle variation over the last 30 years, in contrast with prior findings. Moreover, the MMP shock differs markedly from a textbook monetary policy shock: a contractionary shock leaves interest rates mostly unchanged but persistently lowers headline prices and appreciates the dollar, while temporarily tightening financial conditions and depressing industrial production.

papers.title: Bells and Whistles of Nowcasting Models: Which Matter and When?
papers.abstract: This paper investigates which features of a Bayesian dynamic factor model improve U.S. GDP nowcasts and whether their contribution varies across historical episodes. Using pseudo-real-time information sets for 25 series, we estimate 16 combinations of dynamic heterogeneity, stochastic volatility, time-varying long-run growth, and a multiplicative outlier adjustment. We evaluate their marginal contributions to point, density, and quantile score forecasts using balanced paired factorial contrasts. Dynamic heterogeneity improves point, density, and tail forecasts, and it is the only feature that helps consistently across all three criteria. Stochastic volatility improves density and tail forecasts in some periods but not point forecasts consistently. Time-varying long-run growth lowers squared-error loss in some periods but worsens tail forecasts. The outlier adjustment does not improve point or density forecasts overall, has favorable but imprecisely estimated effects on upper-tail quantile scores during the pandemic, and worsens those scores afterward.

papers.title: Peer Influence in College Applications
papers.abstract: This paper studies how exposure to peers affects college application behavior. We use neighbors who attend different high schools to mitigate concerns about common shocks. Using granular classroom-level data, we find that exposure to peers who have applied to a program increases application rates. Consistent with an information mechanism, there is no additional effect of peers who are admitted. In counterfactuals, the effect is large enough to close urban-rural gaps and gender gaps in applications to selective college programs. We make the (generally NP-hard) application portfolio choice problem tractable using a setting where admission probabilities are observable and conditionally independent.

papers.title: A Macroeconomic Analysis of Household Labor Supply Responses to Large Fiscal Transfers
papers.abstract: The fiscal transfers deployed during the COVID-19 pandemic were unprecedented in scale and strongly progressive. Using CPS/ASEC data, we document that the decline in employment during the pandemic was larger for low-income households and tightly linked to the intensity of transfer receipt, a pattern absent during the Global Financial Crisis. We develop and estimate a two-sector, heterogeneous-household general equilibrium model in which low-income households are borrowing-constrained in normal times but can save out of sufficiently large transfers. Because preferences permit wealth effects on labor supply, transfers both reduce labor supply and raise consumption, and a dollar of transfers is split roughly evenly between the two margins. We find that the effects of transfers are state-dependent: because the borrowing constraint binds more tightly in a deeper recession, the same transfer relaxes a tighter constraint and delivers an employment and consumption response about 40 to 50 percent larger during the pandemic than when the same transfer is introduced in the steady state. In the model, transfers were welfare-improving for recipients, with gains diminishing as transfers increase.
